paragraphs.title: The Empty Vine and the Coming Disaster

easy.explanation: Israel is compared to an empty vine.
easy.q: What is Israel compared to in verse 1?

easy.explanation: The verse says Israel increased the altars according to the multitude of its fruit.
easy.q: What did Israel increase as its fruit increased?

answers: It multiplied its altars and images
It gave the harvest to the poor
medium.explanation: Israel used its prosperity to increase idolatrous worship.
medium.q: What did Israel do with the prosperity represented by its fruit?

medium.explanation: They said, “We have no king,” because they did not fear the LORD.
medium.q: What did Israel claim about its king?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “Thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows.”
medium.q: What sprang up like hemlock in the furrows?

answers: Israel appeared fruitful, but its fruit led to idolatry
Israel was poor, but its fields were fertile
Israel lived in a city, but worked in the wilderness
challenge.explanation: Israel’s outward fruitfulness resulted in more altars rather than faithfulness to God.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown by the image of the vine?

answers: They were wholly devoted to the LORD
They were spiritually divided and therefore guilty
challenge.explanation: A divided heart shows divided loyalty and leaves them guilty before God.
challenge.q: What does “Their heart is divided” imply?

challenge.explanation: They spoke falsely, swearing falsely when making a covenant.
challenge.q: What kind of speech characterized the people?

short_answers.question: Complete the phrase: “Israel is an _____ vine.”
short_answers.explanation: Hosea 10:1 calls Israel an empty vine.

short_answers.question: What did Israel not fear?
short_answers.explanation: They said they had no king because they feared not the LORD.

short_answers.question: What sprang up in the furrows?
short_answers.explanation: Judgment sprang up as hemlock in the furrows.

paragraphs.title: The Calf of Beth-el and Samaria’s Fear

easy.explanation: They would fear because of the calves of Beth-aven.
easy.q: What would the inhabitants of Samaria fear?

easy.explanation: The calf would be carried unto Assyria.
easy.q: Where would the calf be carried?

easy.explanation: The verse says the high places of Aven would be destroyed.
easy.q: What would happen to the high places of Aven?

answers: The calf and its glory would be taken away
The king would build a new altar
medium.explanation: They mourned because the calf’s glory had departed from it.
medium.q: Why would the people and priests mourn?

medium.explanation: Foam on water is unstable and soon disappears.
medium.q: What does “as the foam upon the water” suggest about Samaria’s king?

medium.explanation: The verse says thorn and thistle would come up on the altars.
medium.q: What would grow upon the altars?

answers: The idol could not protect Israel
The idol would receive a new temple
challenge.explanation: The calf was carried away, showing that it could not save or protect Israel.
challenge.q: What does the removal of the calf demonstrate?

answers: As temporary and unable to withstand judgment
As willing servants of the LORD
challenge.explanation: Samaria’s king is compared to foam, emphasizing their disappearance.
challenge.q: How are Samaria and its king portrayed?

answers: Fear and a longing to escape judgment
challenge.explanation: The people ask the mountains and hills to cover them because of terror.
challenge.q: What does the cry, “Cover us,” reveal?

short_answers.question: To what country was the calf carried?
short_answers.explanation: The calf was carried unto Assyria.

short_answers.question: What would come up on the altars?
short_answers.explanation: The abandoned altars would be overgrown with thorn and thistle.

short_answers.question: What did the people ask the mountains to do?
short_answers.explanation: They cried to the mountains, “Cover us.”

paragraphs.title: The Sin of Gibeah and the Yoke upon Israel

easy.explanation: Israel had sinned from the days of Gibeah.
The people would be gathered against them.
easy.q: Who would be gathered against Israel?

easy.explanation: Ephraim is compared to a heifer that is taught.
easy.q: What animal is Ephraim compared to?

answers: Israel’s sin had continued for a long time
medium.explanation: The reference shows that Israel’s sinful pattern reached back to the days of Gibeah.
medium.q: What does the reference to Gibeah show?

medium.explanation: Ephraim is described as a heifer that was taught.
medium.q: What kind of heifer was Ephraim?

medium.explanation: The yoke represents God’s discipline and the burden placed upon Israel.
medium.q: What does the yoke represent in this passage?

answers: Israel had ability, yet needed discipline
Israel was incapable of any work
Israel had already returned completely to God
challenge.explanation: A trained heifer can work properly, but Israel still needed correction and direction.
challenge.q: What tension appears in the image of the trained heifer?

answers: Discipline can direct Israel toward proper service
challenge.explanation: The image of a trained animal suggests that discipline can guide Israel into proper work.
challenge.q: How might discipline relate to restoration?

answers: From continued sin to judgment and imposed discipline
challenge.explanation: The passage recalls sin, announces judgment, and describes the discipline God will impose.
challenge.q: What is the main movement of verses 9–11?

short_answers.question: From what place did Israel’s sins date?
short_answers.explanation: Israel had sinned from the days of Gibeah.

short_answers.question: Who would be gathered against the people?
short_answers.explanation: The passage says the people would be gathered against them.

short_answers.question: What animal represented Ephraim?
short_answers.explanation: Ephraim is compared to a taught heifer.

easy.explanation: They were told, “Sow to yourselves in righteousness.”
easy.q: What were the people told to sow?

easy.explanation: The prophet told them to seek the LORD.
easy.q: Whom were they told to seek?

answers: Their way and their mighty men
easy.explanation: They trusted in their way and in the multitude of their mighty men.

medium.explanation: The verse connects sowing righteousness with reaping mercy.
medium.q: What is connected with sowing righteousness?

medium.explanation: The command pictures preparing the heart and life for a new response to God.
medium.q: What does “break up your fallow ground” mean in context?

medium.explanation: They had plowed wickedness and reaped iniquity.
medium.q: What had Israel actually plowed and reaped?

challenge.explanation: Sowing and reaping illustrate the connection between conduct and its consequences.
challenge.q: What moral principle is expressed through farming imagery?

answers: A change from trusting strength to seeking the LORD
challenge.explanation: The people were called to seek the LORD rather than trust their own power.
challenge.q: What change did the prophet demand?

answers: The call to righteousness is contrasted with Israel’s practice of wickedness
Both verses concern only the weather
challenge.explanation: Verse 12 gives the proper path, while verse 13 describes the sinful path Israel chose.

short_answers.question: What were they told to reap?
short_answers.explanation: They were told, “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy.”

short_answers.question: What ground were they told to break up?
short_answers.explanation: The prophet commanded them to break up their fallow ground.

short_answers.question: What did they eat as the fruit of their conduct?
short_answers.explanation: They had eaten the fruit of lies because they trusted in their own way.

paragraphs.title: The Destruction of the Fortresses and the King’s Disappearance

easy.explanation: A tumult would arise among the people.
easy.q: What would arise among the people?

answers: They would be moved to Judah
easy.explanation: All their fortresses would be spoiled.
easy.q: What would happen to the fortresses?

answers: He would build a new fortress
easy.explanation: The king of Israel would be utterly cut off.
easy.q: What would happen to the king of Israel?

medium.explanation: The destruction is compared with how Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in battle.
medium.q: What event was used as an example of the coming destruction?

medium.explanation: The fortresses would be plundered and destroyed.
medium.q: What does “spoiled” mean in the context of the fortresses?

answers: The calf of Beth-el and Israel’s great wickedness
medium.explanation: Beth-el would bring judgment because of Israel’s great wickedness.
medium.q: What was identified as the cause of the disaster?

answers: The fortresses could not save them and were spoiled
The fortresses became places of worship
challenge.explanation: Despite their fortifications, Israel’s defenses would be destroyed.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between Israel’s fortresses and their fate?

answers: The suddenness of the king’s destruction
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes how quickly the king would be cut off.

answers: Idolatry and self-reliance lead to national destruction
Military strength removes the need to fear God
challenge.explanation: The ending shows that Israel’s wickedness, idolatry, and trust in strength lead to judgment.
challenge.q: How does this conclusion gather together the chapter’s themes?

short_answers.question: What would arise among the people?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people.”

short_answers.question: What city did Shalman spoil?
short_answers.explanation: The fortresses would be spoiled as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel.

short_answers.question: Who would be cut off?
short_answers.explanation: The king of Israel would be utterly cut off.
